draft.title: The dramatic monologue
card: A dramatic monologue is one character speaking aloud to a listener who stays silent. The listener is in the scene, but the reader only hears the speaker.
The speaker is not the writer. The writer invents a character and lets that character talk, so the voice belongs to someone else.
The speaker often reveals more than they mean to. Boasts, excuses and slips can show their pride, fear or guilt, even when they are trying to look good.
Readers work out the truth by noticing the gap between what the speaker says and what the words give away. The silent listener is why the speaker keeps talking.
draft.remember: One character talks, the listener is silent, and the words show more than the speaker intends.

a.q: Which feature makes a text a dramatic monologue?
opts: One character speaks to a listener who does not reply
Two characters trade short lines of spoken dialogue
A narrator describes a character's thoughts in third person
The writer speaks directly to readers about their own life
a.why: A dramatic monologue is built on one character speaking to a silent listener. Dialogue is the tempting wrong answer, because it also has speaking characters, but it needs a reply from the other person.
a.clue: Think about who speaks and who stays quiet.

b.q: Dev tells a silent teacher that he never copied, that he only glanced at Sam's page, and that he was very tired. What does this most likely reveal about Dev?
opts: He feels guilty and is making excuses
He is calm and has nothing to hide
He wants the teacher to speak next
He is giving the writer's own opinion
b.why: Dev denies copying, then adds a glance and tiredness as excuses. This shows guilt he did not mean to show. Calm is tempting because he sounds polite, but the piling up of excuses suggests he is uneasy.
b.clue: Look at what he adds after he denies it.
